procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated October 20, 1982, by the Special Judge rejecting the appellant's application questioning the jurisdiction of the court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed Criminal Revision Application No. 510 of 1982 in the Bombay High Court against the Special Judge's order. A Single Judge referred the application to a Division Bench. The Division Bench rejected the revision application, upholding the Special Judge's competence to take cognizance of the offenses based on a private complaint.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the decision of the Division Bench of the Bombay High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether a private complaint is maintainable before a Special Judge.

law.summary: A fundamental principle of criminal justice is that anyone can initiate criminal proceedings unless a statute specifically provides otherwise.

Section 8(1) of the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1952, specifically empowers a Special Judge to take cognizance of an offense without the case being committed to it, unlike a regular Court of Sessions.
Section 8(3) of the 1952 Act states that the person conducting a prosecution before a Special Judge shall be "deemed to be a public prosecutor."

application.summary: The Court began with the foundational principle that any citizen can set the criminal law in motion. It held that to block this access to justice, a statute must contain a clear and specific provision to that effect, which the 1952 Act lacks.

The Court rejected the argument that a Special Judge, being like a Court of Sessions, cannot take cognizance directly. It pointed to Section 8(1) of the 1952 Act, which explicitly grants the Special Judge the power to take cognizance without commitment, establishing it as a court of original criminal jurisdiction capable of entertaining a private complaint.

The Court also dismissed the concern that allowing private complaints would thwart the objective of a speedy trial. It viewed the procedural steps involved (like examining the complainant) as a way for the judge to test the seriousness of the complaint, not as a bar to its maintainability.

Finally, the Court turned the appellant's argument about the "public prosecutor" on its head. It reasoned that the provision in Section 8(3) (deeming the prosecutor to be a public prosecutor) actually supports the maintainability of a private complaint. If the legislature had intended to ban private complaints, it would have simply mandated that all prosecutions be conducted by a state-appointed public prosecutor. The "deeming" fiction implies the legislature was aware that private complaints could be filed and wanted to grant the person prosecuting the status of a public prosecutor for procedural purposes.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that a private complaint is legally maintainable before a Special Judge. The Court found no provision in the 1952 Act that bars such a complaint and interpreted the Act's specific provisions, particularly Section 8(1) and 8(3), as supporting the Special Judge's jurisdiction to take cognizance of an offense based on a private complaint.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Special Judge has the power to take cognizance of an offence without the accused being committed to him for trial.

law.fact: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure, there are four recognized methods for a criminal court to take cognizance of an offence: 1) upon a complaint, 2) upon a police report, 3) upon information received from another source (for Magistrates), and 4) upon commitment by a Magistrate (for a Court of Sessions).
law.text_snippet: Now the Code of Criminal Procedure prescribed only four methods of taking cognizance of an offence... upon a complaint, or upon a report of the police officer or where the Magistrate himself comes to know of the commiss.ion of offence through some other source and in the case of Sessions Court,upon a commitment by the Magistrate.

law.fact: Section 8(1) of the relevant Act states that a Special Judge may take cognizance of offences without the accused being committed to him for trial.
law.text_snippet: 8 (1): A special Judge may take cognizance of offences without the accused being committed to him for trial, and in trying the accused persons, shall follow the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, for the trial of warrant cases by Magistrates.

application.fact: The Court reasoned that Section 8(1) both positively grants the power to take cognizance and negatively excludes one specific method of doing so.
application.text_snippet: Section 8(1) of 1952 Act says that the special Judge shall take cognizance of an offence and shall not take it on commitment of the accused. The Legislature provided for both the pQsitive and the negative. It posi· tively conferred power On special Judge to take C~gaizance· Of ·offences and it negatively removed any concept of comtnitment.

application.fact: By explicitly stating that a Special Judge can take cognizance "without the accused being committed to him for trial," the law specifically excludes the method of taking cognizance upon commitment, which is typically used by a Court of Sessions.
application.text_snippet: jurisdiction is conferred upon the presiding officer of the Court of special Judge to take cognizance of offences simultaneously excluding one of the four recognised modes of taking cogniz.ance, namely, upon commitment by a Magistrate as set out in Sec, 193

application.fact: The Court concluded that since one of the four methods of taking cognizance is expressly excluded, the Special Judge must necessarily be empowered to use the other recognized methods.
application.text_snippet: the only other method by which the Court of special Judge can take cognizance of an offence for the trial of which it was set up, is any one of the remaining three other methods known to law by which a criminal court would take cognizance of an offence

application.fact: Therefore, a Special Judge can take cognizance of an offence upon receiving a complaint, upon a police report, or upon his own knowledge of the offence being committed.
application.text_snippet: As a necessary corollary, it must appear that the special Judge can take cognizance of offences enumerated in Sec. 6 (l)(a) and (b) upon a complaint or upon a police report or upon his coming to know in some manner of the offence having been com-mitted.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that a Special Judge has the power to take cognizance of an offence without the accused being committed for trial. The Court's reasoning was that Section 8(1) of the Act positively grants the power to take cognizance while simultaneously and specifically excluding only one of the four recognized methods—cognizance upon commitment. Therefore, by necessary implication, the Special Judge is empowered to use any of the other available methods, such as acting on a police report or a private complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a private complaint is maintainable before a Special Judge.
appellant_arguments: A private complaint cannot be entertained by a Special Judge for offences under the 1952 Act.
An investigation under Section 5A of the 1952 Act is a mandatory condition precedent to the Special Judge taking cognizance of an offence.
Section 5A is a crucial safeguard against frivolous, speculative, and tendentious prosecutions of public servants, and allowing private complaints would bypass this safeguard.
respondent_arguments: A private complaint is maintainable before a Special Judge.
A Special Judge can take cognizance of an offence upon information received from any person, not just a police officer, or upon his own knowledge.

The law provides for the person prosecuting a case before a Special Judge (even on a private complaint) to have the status of a public prosecutor, which implies that private complaints are permissible.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Special Judge has the power to take cognizance of an offence without the accused being committed to him for trial.
appellant_arguments: The Special Judge's power to take cognizance is not direct; it is conditional upon the completion of a mandatory investigation under Section 5A.

By arguing that a police investigation under Section 5A is a prerequisite, it implies that a Special Judge cannot take cognizance directly from a complaint, which is a process that bypasses committal proceedings.
respondent_arguments: A Special Judge has the direct power to take cognizance of an offence.

This power can be exercised upon receiving a complaint from a private person, upon information from any other source, or upon the judge's own knowledge, without the need for the case to be committed by another court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is a well-recognized principle of criminal jurisprudence that anyone can set the criminal law into motion, except where the statute creating an offense indicates to the contrary. A Special Judge has the power to take cognizance of an offense upon a private complaint and is not restricted to acting only upon a police report.
obiter: A court should read a statutory section as it is and cannot rewrite it to suit its convenience or interpret it in a manner that renders it useless.
Where a statute requires a certain thing to be done in a certain way, the thing must be done in that way or not at all.
The concept of locus standi is generally foreign to criminal jurisprudence, except where a statute creating an offense provides for the eligibility of the complainant.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Having examined the matter from all the different angles, we are satisfied that the conclusion reached both by the learned special Judge and Division Bench of the Bombay High Court th:it a private complaint filed by the complainant was clearly maintainable and that the cognizance was properly taken, is correct.
legal_tests_applied: It is a well established cannon of construction that the court should read the section as it is and cannot rewrite it to suit its convenience; nor does any cannon of construction permit the court to read the section in such manner as to render it to some extent otiose.
The principle that anyone can set or put the criminal law in motion remains intact unless contra-indicated by a statutory provision.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that an investigation under Sec. 5A is a condition precedent to taking cognizance, stating the contention "does not commend to us and has no foundation in law."

To accept that a private complaint is not maintainable, the court would require an "unambiguous statutory provision," and a "tangled web of argument for drawing a far fetched implication, cannot be a substitute for an express statutory provision."

The appellant's argument to selectively exclude private complaints while allowing cognizance on a police report was dismissed with the reasoning: "One cannot pick and choose as it suits one's convenience. Either all the three. modalities are available or none. And Sec. 8(1) which confers power of taking cognizance does not show any preference."
why_respondent_won: The general principle of criminal jurisprudence is that anyone can initiate proceedings because an offence is against society, and this right cannot be fettered without a specific statutory exception.

The Legislature had multiple opportunities to restrict the Special Judge's power to take cognizance only upon a police report in Sec. 8(1), but it did not do so, implying a broader power of cognizance.

Section 8(3) confers the status of a deemed public prosecutor on a private complainant. The court found this to be an "additional reason" why private complaints must be maintainable, as the provision would otherwise be illogical.
policy_considerations: An offence is not merely an offence committed in relation to the person who suffers harm but is also an offence against society.

The society for its orderly and peaceful development is interested in the punishment of the offender. Therefore, prosecution for serious offences is undertaken in the name of the State representing the people which would exclude any element of private vendatta or vengeance.

Punishment of the offender in the interest of the society being one of the objects behind penal statutes enacted for larger good of the society, right to initiate proceedings cannot be whittled down, circumscribed or fettered by putting it into a straight jacket formula of locus standi unknown to criminal jurisprudence, save and except specific statutory exception.
